title: More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials
gist: BCI Pioneers Coalition, cofounded by early implant recipient Ian Burkhart, published a version-one set of ethics guidelines in 13 categories for brain-computer interface trials, pushing for participant recognition and compensation, participant ownership of brain data free of NDAs/embargoes, and post-trial device maintenance. The guidelines are acknowledged to be vague in places and drawn from a small group, but signal rising participant leverage over how BCI developers run trials.

insights.claim: The BCI Pioneers Coalition, cofounded in 2022 by brain-implant recipient Ian Burkhart, has published ethics guidelines for brain-computer interface trials with recommendations across 13 categories aimed at academics, clinicians, and companies.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: BCI companies running human trials may face a new participant-defined standard of conduct that shapes trial design and costs.
insights.locator: In 2022, Burkhart cofounded BCI Pioneers Coalition

insights.claim: Jennifer Chandler, a University of Ottawa law and neuroethics professor, argues existing clinical-trial ethics rules are insufficient for BCI trials because participants carry an embedded device for years and invest significant time, body, and intellectual effort.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Signals BCI trials may attract bespoke ethical/regulatory expectations beyond standard drug or device trial norms.
insights.quote: These are people who have a device embedded in their brain, are in trials sometimes for years and years
insights.locator: Ethics guidelines for clinical trials already

insights.claim: The guidelines are framed as a first version: some recommendations are vague, may overlap existing ethics standards, lack explicit solutions, and were drawn from a small group because very few people live with BCIs.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Expect the standard to evolve; near-term enforcement power is limited but direction of travel is set.
insights.quote: This is a living document, and this is version one
insights.locator: Some of the guidelines are vague

insights.claim: Ian Burkhart says his BCI trial participation meant lab visits two or three days a week for four hours at a time, equivalent to a part-time job.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Participant labor burden is substantial, implying compensation demands could raise BCI trial costs.
insights.quote: That’s [easily] a part-time job if you just count the hours you’re putting in.
insights.locator: During the trials that Burkhart participated

insights.claim: The guidelines recommend recognizing and compensating BCI trial participants, including potentially listing them as coauthors on scientific publications or naming them publicly as research collaborators, while acknowledging not everyone will want this.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Shifts the participant role from subject to collaborator, which could affect IP, publication and recruitment practices.
insights.locator: Others who find themselves in a similar position

themes.theme: Brain data ownership, privacy and NDAs

insights.claim: The guidelines state brain data should be treated as the participant's personal information, and push for participants to access their own brain data at any time, something not always possible historically.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Data-access rights could constrain how BCI companies hoard neural datasets that underpin their algorithmic edge.
insights.quote: should be understood as the participant’s personal information.
insights.locator: The guidelines state that brain data

insights.claim: Participants want to ensure embargoes or NDAs designed to keep findings from competitors do not stop them from sharing their brain data with their own doctors; Burkhart says firm NDAs are not super common in trials but should be prevented.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Competitive secrecy practices of BCI firms may come under pressure from participant advocacy.
insights.quote: It’s not super common for there to be firm NDAs within a lot of the trials

insights.claim: Privacy sensitivity varies by implant type: motor-control neural data bothered Burkhart little, but participants with speech-decoding implants that turn thoughts into words may feel very differently about storage and analysis of their data.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Thought-to-text BCIs carry higher privacy and reputational risk than motor BCIs.

insights.claim: The guidelines say researchers have a duty to prepare participants for media attention because full anonymity of BCI trial participants may be difficult to maintain given public interest in such technologies.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: High public visibility of BCI trials raises reputational stakes for sponsors.

insights.claim: About five years into Burkhart's implant, funding problems led his research team to tell him the implant would have to be removed and could be reimplanted once funding was secured; it was ultimately removed in 2021 after an infection at the scalp cable site.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Funding fragility directly translates into patient harm and ethical exposure for BCI programs.

insights.claim: Rita Leggett, an Australian woman with an epilepsy brain implant, had the device removed against her will after the company that made it went bust two years later, an act ethicists have described as a potential breach of human rights.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Company failure in neurotech creates human-rights and liability risk, making sponsor solvency a material issue.

insights.claim: The guidelines say researchers should commit to maintaining brain devices for a reasonable period after a trial ends, give participants ample time to prepare for removal surgery, and set aside extra funds to support them.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: If adopted, post-trial maintenance reserves would add to BCI developers' capital requirements.

insights.claim: Burkhart's 2014 implant, a 96-electrode array in the motor cortex wired by cable to a computer that drove an electrode sleeve on his arm, let him pour beads, move delicate objects and play Guitar Hero, though only during lab visits.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Illustrates both early BCI capability and the tethered, lab-bound limits commercial systems must overcome.
